tagline.text: Igorot huts and themed gardens in a pine forest

location.label: Location
location.text: 37 Leonard Wood Road, Baguio (between Wright Park and Teachers Camp)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~300 (per person, covering entrance fee, transport, photo fees and snacks)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), then overland

children.text: Baguio Botanical Garden is a park set in a pine forest along Leonard Wood Road, where you can see traditional Igorot huts, friendship gardens from several countries and a tunnel said to have been dug by Japanese soldiers, all in one place. It is close to downtown and the walking distance is short, so families can drop in without strain.

Baguio Botanical Garden is a city park at 37 Leonard Wood Road in Baguio. It lies between Wright Park and Teachers Camp, so it slots naturally into the usual city sightseeing loop of Mines View Park, The Mansion and Camp John Hay. It is managed by the City Environment and Parks Management Office (CEPMO), and paths and gardens run through the pine forest above the city. At the entrance there is a colorful arch, and inside you will find wooden bridges, ponds, streams and benches.

The park's identity shows in the fact that its name has changed several times. Locals have long called it the "Igorot Village" because of its Cordillera carvings and traditional huts. For decades it was also known as "Centennial Park," marking Baguio's 100th anniversary. One account says it closed in 2021 during the pandemic and for rehabilitation, then reopened after about ten months. One site describes it as drawing roughly 100,000 visitors a month. The figure is not exact, but it gives a sense of how popular the place is in Baguio. A tunnel said to have been dug by Japanese soldiers was closed for a while and is described as having reopened after repairs. Given this history, it is best to check which areas are currently open before you go.

There is far more to see than the name "botanical garden" suggests. There is the Cordillera Village, a collection of traditional Cordillera huts, plus a cactus and succulent garden, a dahlia garden, an orchidarium, a sunflower field, and themed gardens commemorating friendship with the United States, China, Japan, Korea and Thailand. Replicas of Korean and Chinese temples and pavilions are also here, so Korean travelers will meet some familiar scenery. In the Centennial Park area there is also said to be a bronze sculpture by Ben Hur Villanueva depicting the groups who built Baguio. Its biggest strength is that you can sample nature, culture and history in one place.

This guide is for travelers spending a day or half a day in Baguio who want to see the city's sights. Most areas are flat and there are ramps, so getting around is not difficult, and about two hours is enough for a thorough visit. Entrance fees can change under city ordinances, so check the latest announcement before you go. In particular, there was a report that the free-entry period for residents of Baguio and nearby Benguet municipalities ended in February 2026, so visitors from outside should assume they will have to pay.

This area gathers traditional Igorot huts. You can enter some of the huts, and the statues and murals show local history and folklore. Near the front gate there are also photographers who print your photos on site, and shops selling potted plants and seeds if you want to buy plants.
This tunnel, about
long, is said to have been dug by Japanese soldiers during World War II. It is described as having been closed for a while and then reopened, so check before you go.

There are gardens commemorating friendship with the United States, China, Japan, Korea and Thailand, and one account mentions a Canadian garden as well. Replicas of Korean and Chinese temples and pavilions make for good photos. Props such as elephant statues, small Buddhas and a Japanese-style shrine and tunnel are scattered around, so walking a loop and comparing the atmosphere of each country is fun.

There is a bronze sculpture depicting the groups that built Baguio. If you are interested in the city's history, it is worth viewing slowly along with the information boards. Benches are placed throughout, which makes it easy to rest, and ramps make it easier for travelers with limited mobility to move around.
A dahlia garden, an orchidarium, a sunflower field and a cactus and succulent garden are arranged in separate areas. Bloom times differ each year, so check recent photos before you go.

Shops near the entrance sell souvenirs such as woven goods, wood carvings, potted plants and T-shirts, and some craftsmen show their work. Photos in rented Igorot costume are also popular. Near the main gate there are also photographers who print your pictures on the spot, and shops selling potted plants and seeds.
Winding paths, wooden bridges, ponds, streams and benches run among tall pine trees. It is a pleasant place to walk slowly in Baguio's cool weather.

children.text: Enter through the main gate and pay the entrance fee at the ticket booth. First browse the shops and souvenir stalls near the entrance.
Go to the Cordillera Village and look at the Igorot huts, statues and murals.
Walk through the friendship gardens and the area with temple and pavilion replicas, taking photos.
Tour Centennial Park, the flower beds, the orchidarium and the cactus garden in turn.
If the Japanese tunnel is open, go to its entrance, read the notice and take a short walk.
Return to the main gate to buy souvenirs or rest at a nearby coffee shop.
Which areas are open can change from season to season, so ask the staff first.
Have breakfast in downtown Baguio, then take a jeepney heading toward Mines View Park or a taxi to Leonard Wood Road.
Spend about two hours looking around the botanical garden.
Move on toward nearby Teachers Camp, Wright Park or The Mansion.
Return downtown for lunch and shop on Session Road.

Teachers Camp and Wright Park are both on the Leonard Wood Road side, so they are easy to reach by taxi or on foot. In the afternoon, going down to Burnham Park downtown and walking around the lake also fits well.

Baguio is high in elevation and cool all year, and the botanical garden is relatively cool thanks to the shade of the pine forest. Even so, rain is frequent in the wet season and makes walking in the garden unpleasant, so the dry months of November–May are best. Flowers differ by season, so even the same garden feels different depending on the month of your visit.

From November to January it is the Christmas season, and the garden is said to be lit with lights at night. Visitors are especially numerous then, so go early in the morning or choose a weekday. During the Panagbenga Flower Festival in February, the whole city is crowded.

There is no lodging inside the botanical garden, but there are hotels and guesthouses near Teachers Camp and Wright Park. Most travelers stay around Burnham Park or Session Road in downtown Baguio and travel from there.

You can have a simple meal at the coffee shop in the park or at stalls near the front gate, but a proper meal is better eaten back downtown. Baguio also has many Korean restaurants, so if you miss Korean food you can eat it downtown. Bringing snacks and water in advance helps you save money.

If you are more interested in plants and flowers, the Baguio Orchidarium in Burnham Park and the orchidarium at Benguet State University in La Trinidad are also often mentioned. Potted plants, seeds, woven goods, wood carvings, T-shirts and key chains sold at the garden are described as the most common souvenirs.
Admission fees change, so check the latest announcement before you go.
Going early in the morning means fewer people and easier photos. Opening hours are known to be roughly 6:00 to 18:00.
The Japanese tunnel and some areas may be closed depending on circumstances, so ask the staff first.

The garden takes about two hours to cover, so combining it with Teachers Camp or The Mansion makes a half-day route.
Smoking, littering, graffiti and picking flowers are prohibited. Pets are allowed, but owners must clean up after them.

Entrance fees and open areas change with city ordinances and renovation work, so check the latest information before visiting.
The free-entry period for residents of Baguio and nearby Benguet municipalities is reported to have ended at the end of January 2026, so fee policy may keep changing.

It is crowded on public holidays and at year-end, so watch your belongings.
Underground areas such as the Japanese tunnel can be dark and narrow, so bring a phone light.
